bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- OEM concentration risk — Dependence on select OEM partners may expose the Company to changes in OEM strategy, vehicle allocation, margin structures, brand performance and dealership terms. This is structural for a dealership: the Company has no product of its own, and Mercedes-Benz alone contributed approximately 40% of new-car proforma revenue. Mitigation is to strengthen relationships with existing OEM partners while expanding into new and high-growth brands, supported by dealer performance and continued strategic relevance.
- Regulatory and taxation risk, including the pending GST compensation cess matter — Changes in taxation, GST provisions including the pending GST compensation cess matter, emission standards, EV regulations, safety requirements or compliance requirements may affect costs, pricing, operations and near-term profitability. The abolition of the compensation cess during the year created temporary ambiguity around accumulated cess credits at the dealer level and forced one-time discounting to clear cess-impacted inventory. Mitigation is tracking regulatory developments, coordinating with OEMs and industry bodies, and prudent provisioning and compliance.
- Inventory and working capital risk — Inefficient inventory planning or credit cycles may block capital and affect liquidity, particularly across multi-brand operations and during regulatory transitions. Inventory stood at approximately 36 days at end-March 2026, deliberately raised from December levels to protect availability and capture anticipated OEM price increases. Mitigation is disciplined inventory planning, tighter receivables control, OEM-supported channel financing and favourable commercial terms.
- Ramp-up risk on newly added outlets and workshops — Newly added outlets and workshops typically require a gestation period before reaching optimal productivity, and any delay in their ramp-up may affect consolidated margins and return ratios. Workshops opened for Kia, Mahindra & Mahindra and MG Motor remained in ramp-up during the year and operated below the throughput of mature facilities. This is the central execution risk after 18 months of accelerated network expansion.
- Economic and geopolitical risk — Macroeconomic volatility, inflationary pressure, currency movement, geopolitical tensions (including developments in West Asia), fuel-price volatility or higher interest rates may affect discretionary automobile purchases and disrupt supply, weighing on revenue performance. Mitigation is an asset-light model, a brand portfolio spanning price points and segments, and a balance sheet with lower debt.
- Supply chain risk — Disruptions in vehicle or spare-parts availability arising from global shortages, geopolitical events or OEM-level constraints may affect both sales and after-sales performance. Mitigation is close OEM coordination, calibrated inventory buffers and flexible service operations.
- Liquidity risk — Slower vehicle sales or delays in collections may affect the Company's ability to meet short-term obligations. Mitigation is maintaining healthy cash balances, strong operating cash flows, disciplined working-capital practices and established credit lines with financial institutions.
- Technology, digital and cybersecurity risk — Failure to keep pace with digital transformation, including AI-led customer engagement, or disruptions in digital platforms may affect customer experience and operating efficiency; rising digitisation also raises exposure to cyberattacks, data breaches and system downtime. Mitigation is end-to-end digitisation across the customer lifecycle, AI-led process improvement, technology partnerships, cybersecurity protocols, periodic audits, employee-awareness initiatives and real-time monitoring of digital systems and customer data.
- Reputational risk — Adverse customer experiences, service-related concerns or negative perception on social media may affect consumer trust and sales performance — material for a B2C retailer serving over 5,50,000 customers. Mitigation is consistent customer service, stronger post-sale engagement and proactive communication across touchpoints.
- Employee attrition and talent concentration — A structural concentration disclosure rather than a labelled risk: the BRSR reports a permanent-employee turnover rate of 22.63% in 2025-26 (46.95% for female employees), against 33.88% in 2024-25. With roughly 5,120 people across showrooms, workshops and corporate offices and a customer-first service model, retention of technical and customer-facing staff bears directly on workshop throughput and service quality.
- Single-activity and single-geography concentration — A structural concentration disclosure: BRSR Section A reports 100% of turnover from a single main activity (retail trading — sale and distribution of automobiles), with exports nil and no international operations. The Company is wholly exposed to the Indian passenger and commercial vehicle retail cycle, with no product, geographic or export diversification to absorb a domestic downturn.

outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: 2025-26 was a deliberate year of consolidation rather than expansion. After operationalising 23 new outlets in the previous year, Landmark moderated to nine net additions, taking the network to 140 outlets across 29 cities and 12 states (76 sales showrooms and 64 workshops, count as on May 26, 2026). Eight new showrooms were added across Bihar, Gujarat, West Bengal, Madhya Pradesh, Goa and Telangana. Patna, Bihar was the only new market entry, where the Company opened Bihar's first Mercedes-Benz showroom and workshop, taking its longest-standing luxury partnership into a state it had not served before. Most other additions deepened existing clusters: MG Select showroom and workshop in Ahmedabad and Kolkata, an MG Motor showroom in Goa, a Kia workshop in Hyderabad, a small Mahindra & Mahindra outlet in Hyderabad, and a Mercedes-Benz outlet in Bhopal. New workshops were commissioned for Kia, Mahindra & Mahindra and MG Motor, expanding the service footprint; these facilities remained in ramp-up during the year and operated below the throughput of mature workshops, with utilisation expected to improve as the car parc of the newer brands expands. Against this, the Company rationalised underperforming locations, exiting its Volkswagen operations in Delhi-NCR (one showroom and one workshop) with effect from March 31, 2026, while continuing as Volkswagen's dealer in the profitable Gujarat market. Looking ahead, management has stated that 2026-27 will remain focused on consolidation, with growth continuing through facilities already under implementation, including BYD in Pune and additional after-sales capacity for Mahindra & Mahindra; select opportunities may be pursued where the strategic rationale and financial potential are attractive, but the pace of expansion will be measured. Capital expenditure is not expected to remain at the elevated levels seen during the expansion phase. The Company financed its network through internal accruals without raising new long-term debt or diluting equity, and after two years of elevated investment intends a measured approach to capex with greater emphasis on network productivity and selective expansion. The Board also approved a scheme of amalgamation of wholly-owned subsidiary Landmark (East) Private Limited with the Company, subject to requisite approvals, to support operational simplification and cost efficiency. Approximately one-fourth of the Company's presence has historically been built through acquisitions under an asset-light model. outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Premiumisation of the Indian passenger vehicle market: premium and luxury PVs continue to gain ground over entry-level cars on rising affluence and preference for higher-end variants; the average selling price of new vehicles rose to approximately Rs 21.96 Lacs in 2025-26 from Rs 20.79 Lacs, and Mercedes-Benz average selling price reached a record level.
- GST 2.0, effective September 2025, lowered effective tax rates and abolished the compensation cess, materially improving vehicle affordability; management expects the full-year benefit of GST rationalisation to support 2026-27 demand. GST on spare parts fell to 18% from 28%, improving the competitiveness of authorised workshops against unorganised garages.
- Maturation of newly commissioned outlets is the key margin lever: outlets added during the recent expansion phase are expected to contribute more substantially as they mature, providing operating leverage; newer franchises narrowed the profitability gap with established businesses as scale improved.
- Newly added brands (Kia, Mahindra & Mahindra, MG Motor) contributed approximately 20% of proforma revenue and are rising as a share, reflecting a deliberate portfolio transformation.
- After-sales mix: the after-sales business crossed the Rs 10,000 Million annual revenue mark for the first time, a recurring, higher-margin stream expected to grow as the vehicle parc of the newer brands expands; recently opened workshops are still ramping and management expects margins to return towards historical levels as the parc builds and those workshops mature.
- Margin improvement ahead is expected from continued cost optimisation, higher contribution from matured outlets, improved workshop throughput, better realisations from renegotiated arrangements with insurance partners and vendors, and a growing after-sales mix.
- EV adoption: EVs contributed over 24% of the Company's new-car sales on a proforma revenue basis, above the industry's own PV EV penetration of 4.25%; management expects electric mobility to capture a rising share of the PV market over the medium term as charging networks expand and battery costs fall.
- Fragmentation of Indian auto dealership: organised retailers account for a relatively small share of overall industry volumes compared with developed markets, leaving headroom to scale through selective organic expansion and acquisition-led growth.
- Lower interest rates support vehicle demand directly through financing costs — the RBI brought the policy rate to 5.25% by December 2025 and maintained a neutral stance, alongside income-tax relief in the Union Budget 2025-26.
- Trade agreements — the India-EU FTA concluded January 2026, the India-UK CETA effective July 15, 2026 and the interim India-US framework — may support improved pricing flexibility and enable the introduction of select premium and imported models over the medium term, particularly for brands where Landmark has a strong presence; EVs are expected to remain outside the initial tariff reductions.
- Shift towards SUVs and utility vehicles, now the principal growth engine and the majority of PV sales, keeps demand tilted to larger, feature-rich, higher-value models.
- Allied revenue streams — finance, insurance, accessories and pre-owned vehicles — support higher revenue per customer, deeper lifecycle engagement and a stronger margin profile.
- The pre-owned business is deliberately measured near-term: GST-led improvement in new-car affordability narrowed the new-versus-used price gap and OEM discounting added volatility to used-vehicle valuations, so the Company moderated activity and prioritised pricing discipline over volume, with expansion to be pursued as conditions stabilise.
- Industry outlook for 2026-27 is constructive but watchful: dealer sentiment is positive with FADA indicating nearly three-fourths of dealers expect growth, and early 2026-27 retail trends were encouraging in April and June 2026, tempered by geopolitical conflict in West Asia, fuel-price and currency volatility, supply-chain constraints and selective softness in entry-level demand.
- Structural runway: India remains the third-largest passenger vehicle market globally with among the lowest vehicle penetration, and luxury cars still represent a small share of India's overall PV market, leaving long-term headroom for growth.

risks.note: Dependence on select OEM partners may expose the Company to changes in OEM strategy, vehicle allocation, margin structures, brand performance and dealership terms. This is structural for a dealership: the Company has no product of its own, and Mercedes-Benz alone contributed approximately 40% of new-car proforma revenue. Mitigation is to strengthen relationships with existing OEM partners while expanding into new and high-growth brands, supported by dealer performance and continued strategic relevance.

Changes in taxation, GST provisions including the pending GST compensation cess matter, emission standards, EV regulations, safety requirements or compliance requirements may affect costs, pricing, operations and near-term profitability. The abolition of the compensation cess during the year created temporary ambiguity around accumulated cess credits at the dealer level and forced one-time discounting to clear cess-impacted inventory. Mitigation is tracking regulatory developments, coordinating with OEMs and industry bodies, and prudent provisioning and compliance.
risks.risk: Regulatory and taxation risk, including the pending GST compensation cess matter

risks.note: Inefficient inventory planning or credit cycles may block capital and affect liquidity, particularly across multi-brand operations and during regulatory transitions. Inventory stood at approximately 36 days at end-March 2026, deliberately raised from December levels to protect availability and capture anticipated OEM price increases. Mitigation is disciplined inventory planning, tighter receivables control, OEM-supported channel financing and favourable commercial terms.

Newly added outlets and workshops typically require a gestation period before reaching optimal productivity, and any delay in their ramp-up may affect consolidated margins and return ratios. Workshops opened for Kia, Mahindra & Mahindra and MG Motor remained in ramp-up during the year and operated below the throughput of mature facilities. This is the central execution risk after 18 months of accelerated network expansion.

risks.note: Macroeconomic volatility, inflationary pressure, currency movement, geopolitical tensions (including developments in West Asia), fuel-price volatility or higher interest rates may affect discretionary automobile purchases and disrupt supply, weighing on revenue performance. Mitigation is an asset-light model, a brand portfolio spanning price points and segments, and a balance sheet with lower debt.

Disruptions in vehicle or spare-parts availability arising from global shortages, geopolitical events or OEM-level constraints may affect both sales and after-sales performance. Mitigation is close OEM coordination, calibrated inventory buffers and flexible service operations.

Slower vehicle sales or delays in collections may affect the Company's ability to meet short-term obligations. Mitigation is maintaining healthy cash balances, strong operating cash flows, disciplined working-capital practices and established credit lines with financial institutions.

Failure to keep pace with digital transformation, including AI-led customer engagement, or disruptions in digital platforms may affect customer experience and operating efficiency; rising digitisation also raises exposure to cyberattacks, data breaches and system downtime. Mitigation is end-to-end digitisation across the customer lifecycle, AI-led process improvement, technology partnerships, cybersecurity protocols, periodic audits, employee-awareness initiatives and real-time monitoring of digital systems and customer data.

risks.note: Dependence on select OEM partners may expose the Company to changes in OEM strategy, vehicle allocation, margin structures, brand performance and dealership terms. This is structural for a dealership: the Company has no product of its own, and Mercedes-Benz alone contributed approximately 40% of new-car proforma revenue. Mitigation is to strengthen relationships with existing OEM partners while expanding into new and high-growth brands, supported by dealer performance and continued strategic relevance.

risks.risk: Regulatory and taxation risk, including the pending GST compensation cess matter
risks.note: Changes in taxation, GST provisions including the pending GST compensation cess matter, emission standards, EV regulations, safety requirements or compliance requirements may affect costs, pricing, operations and near-term profitability. The abolition of the compensation cess during the year created temporary ambiguity around accumulated cess credits at the dealer level and forced one-time discounting to clear cess-impacted inventory. Mitigation is tracking regulatory developments, coordinating with OEMs and industry bodies, and prudent provisioning and compliance.

Inefficient inventory planning or credit cycles may block capital and affect liquidity, particularly across multi-brand operations and during regulatory transitions. Inventory stood at approximately 36 days at end-March 2026, deliberately raised from December levels to protect availability and capture anticipated OEM price increases. Mitigation is disciplined inventory planning, tighter receivables control, OEM-supported channel financing and favourable commercial terms.

risks.risk: Ramp-up risk on newly added outlets and workshops
risks.note: Newly added outlets and workshops typically require a gestation period before reaching optimal productivity, and any delay in their ramp-up may affect consolidated margins and return ratios. Workshops opened for Kia, Mahindra & Mahindra and MG Motor remained in ramp-up during the year and operated below the throughput of mature facilities. This is the central execution risk after 18 months of accelerated network expansion.

Macroeconomic volatility, inflationary pressure, currency movement, geopolitical tensions (including developments in West Asia), fuel-price volatility or higher interest rates may affect discretionary automobile purchases and disrupt supply, weighing on revenue performance. Mitigation is an asset-light model, a brand portfolio spanning price points and segments, and a balance sheet with lower debt.

Disruptions in vehicle or spare-parts availability arising from global shortages, geopolitical events or OEM-level constraints may affect both sales and after-sales performance. Mitigation is close OEM coordination, calibrated inventory buffers and flexible service operations.

Slower vehicle sales or delays in collections may affect the Company's ability to meet short-term obligations. Mitigation is maintaining healthy cash balances, strong operating cash flows, disciplined working-capital practices and established credit lines with financial institutions.

Failure to keep pace with digital transformation, including AI-led customer engagement, or disruptions in digital platforms may affect customer experience and operating efficiency; rising digitisation also raises exposure to cyberattacks, data breaches and system downtime. Mitigation is end-to-end digitisation across the customer lifecycle, AI-led process improvement, technology partnerships, cybersecurity protocols, periodic audits, employee-awareness initiatives and real-time monitoring of digital systems and customer data.

Adverse customer experiences, service-related concerns or negative perception on social media may affect consumer trust and sales performance — material for a B2C retailer serving over 5,50,000 customers. Mitigation is consistent customer service, stronger post-sale engagement and proactive communication across touchpoints.

A structural concentration disclosure rather than a labelled risk: the BRSR reports a permanent-employee turnover rate of 22.63% in 2025-26 (46.95% for female employees), against 33.88% in 2024-25. With roughly 5,120 people across showrooms, workshops and corporate offices and a customer-first service model, retention of technical and customer-facing staff bears directly on workshop throughput and service quality.

A structural concentration disclosure: BRSR Section A reports 100% of turnover from a single main activity (retail trading — sale and distribution of automobiles), with exports nil and no international operations. The Company is wholly exposed to the Indian passenger and commercial vehicle retail cycle, with no product, geographic or export diversification to absorb a domestic downturn.

- EV adoption: EVs contributed over 24% of the Company's new-car sales on a proforma revenue basis, above the industry's own PV EV penetration of 4.25%; management expects electric mobility to capture a rising share of the PV market over the medium term as charging networks expand and battery costs fall.
- Fragmentation of Indian auto dealership: organised retailers account for a relatively small share of overall industry volumes compared with developed markets, leaving headroom to scale through selective organic expansion and acquisition-led growth.
- Lower interest rates support vehicle demand directly through financing costs — the RBI brought the policy rate to 5.25% by December 2025 and maintained a neutral stance, alongside income-tax relief in the Union Budget 2025-26.
- Trade agreements — the India-EU FTA concluded January 2026, the India-UK CETA effective July 15, 2026 and the interim India-US framework — may support improved pricing flexibility and enable the introduction of select premium and imported models over the medium term, particularly for brands where Landmark has a strong presence; EVs are expected to remain outside the initial tariff reductions.
- Shift towards SUVs and utility vehicles, now the principal growth engine and the majority of PV sales, keeps demand tilted to larger, feature-rich, higher-value models.
- Allied revenue streams — finance, insurance, accessories and pre-owned vehicles — support higher revenue per customer, deeper lifecycle engagement and a stronger margin profile.
- The pre-owned business is deliberately measured near-term: GST-led improvement in new-car affordability narrowed the new-versus-used price gap and OEM discounting added volatility to used-vehicle valuations, so the Company moderated activity and prioritised pricing discipline over volume, with expansion to be pursued as conditions stabilise.
- Industry outlook for 2026-27 is constructive but watchful: dealer sentiment is positive with FADA indicating nearly three-fourths of dealers expect growth, and early 2026-27 retail trends were encouraging in April and June 2026, tempered by geopolitical conflict in West Asia, fuel-price and currency volatility, supply-chain constraints and selective softness in entry-level demand.
- Structural runway: India remains the third-largest passenger vehicle market globally with among the lowest vehicle penetration, and luxury cars still represent a small share of India's overall PV market, leaving long-term headroom for growth.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: 2025-26 was a deliberate year of consolidation rather than expansion. After operationalising 23 new outlets in the previous year, Landmark moderated to nine net additions, taking the network to 140 outlets across 29 cities and 12 states (76 sales showrooms and 64 workshops, count as on May 26, 2026). Eight new showrooms were added across Bihar, Gujarat, West Bengal, Madhya Pradesh, Goa and Telangana. Patna, Bihar was the only new market entry, where the Company opened Bihar's first Mercedes-Benz showroom and workshop, taking its longest-standing luxury partnership into a state it had not served before. Most other additions deepened existing clusters: MG Select showroom and workshop in Ahmedabad and Kolkata, an MG Motor showroom in Goa, a Kia workshop in Hyderabad, a small Mahindra & Mahindra outlet in Hyderabad, and a Mercedes-Benz outlet in Bhopal. New workshops were commissioned for Kia, Mahindra & Mahindra and MG Motor, expanding the service footprint; these facilities remained in ramp-up during the year and operated below the throughput of mature workshops, with utilisation expected to improve as the car parc of the newer brands expands. Against this, the Company rationalised underperforming locations, exiting its Volkswagen operations in Delhi-NCR (one showroom and one workshop) with effect from March 31, 2026, while continuing as Volkswagen's dealer in the profitable Gujarat market. Looking ahead, management has stated that 2026-27 will remain focused on consolidation, with growth continuing through facilities already under implementation, including BYD in Pune and additional after-sales capacity for Mahindra & Mahindra; select opportunities may be pursued where the strategic rationale and financial potential are attractive, but the pace of expansion will be measured. Capital expenditure is not expected to remain at the elevated levels seen during the expansion phase. The Company financed its network through internal accruals without raising new long-term debt or diluting equity, and after two years of elevated investment intends a measured approach to capex with greater emphasis on network productivity and selective expansion. The Board also approved a scheme of amalgamation of wholly-owned subsidiary Landmark (East) Private Limited with the Company, subject to requisite approvals, to support operational simplification and cost efficiency. Approximately one-fourth of the Company's presence has historically been built through acquisitions under an asset-light model. Separately, the Company commissioned its first rooftop solar plant during the year as part of an environmental strategy carrying a net-zero target set for 2035.

management_tone.title: Management tone
management_tone.body: Confident but disciplined — repeatedly urges judging the business annually, not quarterly. "Year of consolidation / reap benefits / get profits back." Cost focus emphasized strongly. Candid on VW exit, BYD quota issue, one-time nature of inventory gain, and Indian growth story "intact and kicking."

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- India's pioneer in organised auto retail — first to build a multi-brand, multi-location platform in the premium and luxury vehicle space and the first of its kind to list on Indian stock exchanges, among the few organised players consolidating a fragmented retail landscape.
- Robust, long-tenured OEM partnerships — recognised among the leading dealers in India for Mercedes-Benz, Volkswagen, BYD, Honda and Jeep and among the top players for MG Motor, with associations running 28 years (Honda), 18 years (Mercedes-Benz and Volkswagen) and 14 years (Ashok Leyland).
- Diversified 11-brand portfolio spanning premium, luxury, EV and commercial categories, which reduces concentration risk across individual OEMs, geographies and vehicle segments.
- New-energy-ready portfolio — with BYD, Mahindra & Mahindra and MG Motor as pillars, EVs contributed over 24% of sales during the year, well above the industry's own penetration.
- Integrated, margin-accretive after-sales engine — a stable, high-margin, annuity-like revenue stream that crossed the 10,000 Million rupee mark for the first time, counterbalancing the cyclicality of new-vehicle sales and deepening customer retention.
- Full-lifecycle integrated platform — new cars, after-sales and car care, pre-owned, finance and insurance keep the customer with one company from purchase to resale, building recurring revenue.
- Asset-light operating model combining organic expansion with well-executed acquisitions; approximately one-fourth of its presence has been built through acquisitions, enabling faster market access.
- Inventory discipline and cost control, with employee costs moderating to 4.2% of proforma revenue from 4.4% and other operating expenses declining to 3.8% from 4.0%.
- Strong governance including separation of ownership and management, and a resilient, tech-enabled, execution-driven business model with AI-based calling introduced in contact centres.
- Scale of customer relationships — more than 5,50,000 customers served across nearly three decades.

risks.title: Risks
risks.body:
- **OEM dependence / concentration:** Standalone profit heavily Mercedes-linked; quotas (BYD CBU 2,500-unit cap), OEM supply challenges, OEM price/strategy decisions all flow through. No OEM margin renegotiation so far, but mgmt "wait and watch."
- Macro/geopolitical ("war"), FOREX (drives OEM price hikes + spare costs), CV demand hesitancy.
- **GST/cess overhang:** Cess matter pending before Supreme Court (no cess on vehicles currently); had to liquidate cess-laden stock earlier (margin pressure noted in H1).
- After-sales 20% margin may not persist (10-yr avg ~18%).
- EV transition modestly dilutive to long-run service revenue (~12–14% per global study).

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body:
- ~47% of service income is insurance-funded accident repair → structurally protected and EV-resilient (battery replacement more expensive than ICE repair).
- ASP "price-hike benefit" is explicitly a one-time gain on held stock, not a recurring margin lift — important for modeling.
- Standalone (Mercedes-heavy) PAT recovered INR 7 cr → INR 12 cr; quarter bonuses (sales & after-sales) cause lumpy quarterly comparisons.
- A "promoter" reclassifying to non-promoter category holds zero shares (family separation) — no real overhang.
- Mercedes measured by per-car realization (ASP up, units flat/down on VAHAN) with VAHAN lag in some states (Telangana etc.) — VAHAN can understate.

strategy.title: Strategies (RHP)
strategy.body:
- Consolidate rather than expand: after 18 months of accelerated network expansion, make the capacity already built work harder — sweat existing assets, let newly commissioned outlets stabilise and mature, and restore profitability to previously delivered levels.
- Improve asset productivity and return ratios — deepen established clusters, increase workshop utilisation, lift outlet throughput and convert scale into operating leverage rather than adding new markets.
- Anchor growth in capital efficiency: finance the network through internal accruals without raising new long-term debt or diluting …

challenges.title: Challenges → Beneficiaries ✅/⭐
challenges.body:
- ✅ EV penetration rising → BYD/MG/Mahindra portfolio + insurance-funded accident-repair after-sales largely insulates Landmark's service annuity.
- ⭐ OEM India-localization wave (Jeep-Tata, Honda 10 launches, Renault multi-launch, Mercedes 40-product cycle) → Landmark as multi-brand, largest-partner dealer is a direct beneficiary of the product onslaught.

themes.title: Auto OEM cycle - CV replacement & PV premiumization
themes.need: GST 2.0 rate rationalization plus an aged CV fleet still frames the replacement cycle, but Q1FY27's real signal is 2W OEMs EXPANDING margin through a commodity shock. TVSMOTOR sold 1.63mn units (+28%) on INR 13,896cr revenue (+38%) while lifting EBITDA margin 30bps to 12.8% having absorbed a ~4% commodity shock with only ~1.5% of price increase (CARE upgraded it AA+ to AAA), and committed 2W capacity from 6.8mn to 8.3mn by Q4FY27. BAJAJ-AUTO set volume/revenue/EBITDA records with margin at 20.9% (+110bps) through ~4.5% commodity inflation AND ~10% of volume lost to a ransomware shutdown, with EV now 30% of domestic revenue at double-digit EBITDA and Chetak EBITDA-positive - a scaled, profitable EV second engine. Commercial mobility is electrifying fastest: TVSMOTOR's 3W EV penetration crossed 40% for the first time. ASHOKLEY's all-time-high CV volumes (220k units, MHCV share 30.8%) carry the CV leg with defence + Switch EV optionality; TMCV/TMPV/SMLMAH/ESCORTS on CV/tractors; APOLLOTYRE/JKTYRE/BALKRISIND/MRF on tyres.
themes.driver: Capacity commissioning against demand (TVSMOTOR 2W to 8.3mn by Q4FY27, BAJAJ-AUTO 7m to 9m+ units); 3W/2W EV penetration inflection; GST-2.0 price-cut demand, aged-fleet replacement and festive 2W/PV.
